analysis.one_liner: Allows Americans to import prescription drugs from certain countries with comparable safety standards for personal use.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to a House health subcommittee two days after its introduction and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let individuals buy prescription drugs from a list of countries that the FDA determines have safety standards at least as strict as America's, including Canada, Australia, Japan, and European countries. It would allow personal imports of up to a 90-day supply, shipped by a licensed pharmacist, with a valid prescription, excluding controlled substances. The purpose is to let Americans access lower foreign prices for the same drugs.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who pay high out-of-pocket prescription drug prices, especially those buying brand-name drugs not covered by insurance or facing high copays. Today, US law generally bars importing drugs from abroad except by the manufacturer, which protects the higher prices US consumers pay. This bill would carve out a personal-use exception for imports from vetted countries.

how_it_helps.text: Allows individuals to import prescription drugs from countries the FDA certifies as having safety standards at least as protective as US standards, including Canada, Australia, Israel, Japan, New Zealand, Switzerland, South Africa, and European countries.

Limits personal imports to a 90-day supply shipped directly to the consumer or imported by the consumer, dispensed by a licensed pharmacist and accompanied by a valid prescription, and excludes controlled substances.

The bill's stated purpose is 'to reduce prescription drug costs by allowing the importation and reimportation of certain drugs,' by letting a person other than the manufacturer import or reimport qualifying drugs despite current restrictions in the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, which currently benefit from a system in which the same drug sells for more in the US than in Canada or Europe and personal importation is generally barred. Lower-price imports would erode the price premium US consumers pay. The FDA would also bear the work of certifying which countries qualify.

drawbacks.text: Drug-safety advocates have long warned that imported drugs can be counterfeit, mishandled, or mislabeled; the bill addresses this by restricting imports to FDA-certified countries with equivalent standards and requiring licensed pharmacists and valid prescriptions, but critics argue the supply chain outside US oversight still carries risk.

Savings are limited in scope: imports are capped at a 90-day supply for personal use, controlled substances are excluded, and patients must obtain a valid prescription, so it is not a systemic fix for US drug prices and could raise concerns about foreign countries' drug supplies being drawn on.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers facing high US prices, the benefit is straightforward: access to the same FDA-comparable drugs at lower foreign prices. The safety risk is managed by the bill's design, which limits imports to countries with equivalent standards, licensed dispensing, and small personal-use quantities. The cost falls on drug makers' US revenue, not on consumers.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health from February 2017 until the Congress ended, without a hearing or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Keith Ellison introduced the bill on February 7, 2017, joined by Rep. Dana Rohrabacher, a Republican, giving it one sponsor from each party.
Two days after introduction, on February 10, 2017, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health of the House Energy and Commerce Committee.
The bill took no further action of any kind for the rest of the 115th Congress: no subcommittee hearing, no markup, no full committee vote, and no House floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers, which kept the current ban on personal drug importation that protects higher US prices; consumers who pay those prices gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Keith Ellison
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Personal Drug Importation Fairness Act of 2017 on February 7, 2017.

for.name: Rep. Dana Rohrabacher
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as its sole cosponsor, making it a bipartisan introduction.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Health Subcommittee on February 10, 2017 and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Greg Walden
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, never brought the bill to a hearing, markup, or committee vote; it died in subcommittee.

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers
against.role: Industry whose market depends on the importation ban the bill would lift
against.what_they_did: Opposed personal drug importation measures, which industry groups have consistently fought in Congress because they erode the US price premium; the industry's opposition was reflected in the committee's inaction.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only support on the record is one Democrat sponsor and one Republican cosponsor; no recorded votes or hearing transcripts exist to measure partisan support either way.

industries.note: Personal importation from countries where the same drugs sell for less would cut into the price premium these companies charge US consumers. The bill's defeat preserves that premium, which shows up as higher out-of-pocket drug costs for Americans.

The bill would create a legal channel for licensed pharmacists in qualified countries to ship up to 90-day supplies directly to US consumers, expanding their customer base. Their lower prices are what deliver the savings to patients.
